paper_title: LeanPRM: Lean-Grounded Process Supervision for Natural Language Proof Verification

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: AI systems now write long and difficult mathematical proofs, and checking their step-by-step validity is becoming a bottleneck. A learned verifier could check proofs cheaply, but training one requires a correctness label on every step, and such labels are hard to obtain for open-ended proofs. Existing methods take them from human annotators, which is costly, or derive them from final answers, which proofs do not have, and formalizing each proof in Lean requires expert effort. We introduce LeanPRM, a framework that uses the Lean proof assistant to create step-level labels for natural-language proofs. A model writes a natural-language proof together with a paired formal proof, without feedback from Lean. Lean then labels every step, and a second model discards failures caused only by the formal syntax, so that the negative labels mark errors in the mathematics. LeanPRM contains 10,634 proofs with 152K labeled steps and no human annotation. A Qwen3-4B verifier trained on LeanPRM raises exact step-label accuracy on a held-out set of 200 proofs (LeanPRM-Bench) from 48.2 to 74.7, as opposed to 60.3 when the same base model is trained on PRM800K. It also selects better proofs in best-of-N selection on IMO-level problems, and outperforms the PRM800K-trained verifier on three of four external verification benchmarks. Training on LeanPRM improves verifiers at every size from 0.6B to 8B parameters on LeanPRM-Bench, Hard2Verify and IMO-GradingBench. Given the labels need no human annotation, LeanPRM can grow with the supply of formal statements, offering a path to step-level feedback on AI-generated proofs that are hard for humans to check.

sections.title: 1 Introduction
sections.content: As AI systems become more capable, they are increasingly able to produce long and difficult mathematical proofs, including solutions to long-standing open problems [OpenAI, 2026] and complete machine-checked proofs of major theorems such as Fermats Last Theorem [Anthropic, 2026]. At the same time, it is becoming harder to verify the correctness of these proofs. Existing verifiers, including outcome and process reward models, were built for problems with short checkable final answer [Lightman et al., 2023, Rahman et al., 2025, Wang et al., 2023], whereas proof has no final answer to check; its correctness lies in whether every step follows from the ones before it. Formal verification in proof assistant such as Lean offers an alternative, but translating an informal proof into formal language is itself difficult and requires expert-level effort. As result, evaluating the proofs that AI systems produce is hard, especially for non-experts, and reliable supervision for training future systems is scarce. Correspondence to: rlafuente@utexas.edu, salman@nyu.edu, pi390@nyu.edu 1 Figure 1: Overview of LeanPRM, with one example from the corpus running through it. Top row: Stage 1 writes proof attempt from the theorem statement alone, each natural-language step paired with its formal step, and Lean checks the steps in order. Bottom row: Stage 2 decides whether the first failure lies in the mathematics or only in the formal syntax (syntax failures are patched and rechecked once), and the verifier is trained on the natural-language steps and their labels only. Here step 5 asserts without justification that conjugation by fixes x, so steps 1 to 4 are labeled correct and steps 5 and 6 incorrect. verifier trained on natural-language proofs could check them cheaply, but training it requires correctness label on every step, and such labels are scarce for open-ended proofs. Human annotation is expensive even for short solutions, as PRM800K needed about 800,000 step labels [Lightman et al., 2023], and proofs are harder to judge. Automatic labels that score step by whether its continuations reach the correct final answer [Wang et al., 2023] do not apply when there is no final answer. We introduce LeanPRM, framework that uses the Lean proof assistant [de Moura and Ullrich, 2021], an exact mechanical checker, to create these labels. Each natural-language step is paired with formal step, Lean checks the formal step, and the result becomes the label of the natural-language step. Lean is used once, to build the training data, and the trained verifier reads only natural language. We explain how we build the data in Figure 1 and give the full procedure in Section 2. For each theorem statement we ask model to prove it in single pass, writing each step in natural language together with its corresponding Lean step. The model never sees the output of running the Lean step it generated. If it could, it would repair its mistakes or give up, and we would lose the genuine errors we wish to label. As result, the errors in LeanPRM are the models own, and we dont have to prompt it in order to induce them. Following this we run Lean on the formal proof. Steps before the first failing Lean step are labeled correct, and the failing step and every later step are labeled 2 incorrect. step can also fail for purely formal reasons while the mathematics is sound, so we use second model call to read the Lean error message, repair syntax errors once and classify the failure. We keep only proofs whose first failure is mathematical error. In total we obtain 10,634 labeled proofs with 152,005 step labels and no human annotation, which we release together with LeanPRM-Bench, held-out benchmark of 200 proofs. In our experiments, we use LeanPRM to train verifier models for natural language. The results show improved performance relative to the same training process applied to the human labels of PRM800K. With the same model, training recipe and number of updates, LeanPRM-Verifier-4B beats the PRM800K-trained verifier on four of five benchmarks, by 14.4 points of exact step-label accuracy on LeanPRM-Bench and by 9.7 and 9.4 points on Hard2Verify and IMO-GradingBench. It also picks correct proofs more often than random selection in best-of-N on IMO-level problems, where the PRM800K verifier stays close to chance. Training on LeanPRM improves verifiers at every size we tried, from 0.6B to 8B parameters, on LeanPRM-Bench, Hard2Verify and IMO-GradingBench. We provide detailed results in Section 3. We make three contributions. LeanPRM, to our knowledge the first framework that uses Lean to produce step-level correctness labels for natural-language proofs at scale, and its corpus of 10,634 labeled proofs (Section 2). LeanPRM-Bench, held-out benchmark of 200 natural-language proofs with step labels, which we release for evaluating proof verifiers (Section 2.2). controlled evaluation showing that, with the same recipe and training budget, verifiers trained on Lean-grounded labels outperform verifiers trained on human labels on four of five benchmarks, select better proofs at test time on IMO-level problems, and improve at every model size from 0.6B to 8B on three of the five benchmarks (Section 3).

sections.title: 2 LeanPRM: Lean-Grounded Process Supervision
sections.content: We introduce LeanPRM, framework for generating natural-language proofs with correctness labels on every step, grounded in Lean. Lean is proof assistant that checks formal proofs and tactics are commands used to construct them [de Moura and Ullrich, 2021]. The framework has two stages (Figure 1): (i) model writes natural-language proof together with formal proof in Lean, pairing each natural-language step with the corresponding Lean tactic, and (ii) Lean compiles the formal proof and second model reviews the result. If compilation failed, the second model decides whether the failure is mathematical error or only syntax error, which it attempts to repair once. If compilation succeeded, it checks that the natural-language steps state the same mathematics as the formal proof. Up to the first failure, each natural-language step is labeled by the outcome of its tactic. Every step subsequent to the first failure is labeled incorrect. Stage 1: Proof generation. We start from about 17,800 distinct theorem statements from public formal corpora, mostly from NuminaMath-LEAN [Wang et al., 2025] and Lean-Workbook [Lin et al., 2025a, Ying et al., 2024] (Figure 2, with all sources listed in Appendix B). The seed statements span algebra, inequalities, number theory, and existence problems, with some calculus and combinatorics. NuminaMath statements are selected from the hard tier assigned by Gemini Flash-Lite, and Lean-Workbook is sampled by statement category without difficulty labels. For each statement, one model call writes proof attempt as numbered steps, each sentence of ordinary mathematical prose paired with the formal step that carries it out (prompt in Appendix I). The model sees only the statement and generates proof in one shot, without receiving feedback from the checker. The 3 Figure 2: Composition of LeanPRM. Left: sources of the 10,634 theorems. Right: error class of the first failing step in each of the 4,264 incorrect proofs. Bars show percentages of incorrect proofs. Every incorrect proof fails first at mathematical error, most often an unjustified assumption. model is always asked to prove the theorem and is never instructed to make mistake, so every error in LeanPRM is one the model made while genuinely trying to produce proof. Because many statements were selected for difficulty (Appendix B), many of these genuine attempts fail. We used Claude Sonnet 5 for most theorems and Claude Opus 4.8 for an earlier subset. Stage 2: Verification and error classification. The frozen formal proof is compiled with Lean 4 and Mathlib (both v4.25.0-rc2), and no compiler output is shown to the generator. Because each sentence was written with its own formal step, compilation error points to exactly one step. formal step can fail to compile even when the mathematics is right, so second and final model call reads the statement, the steps and the compiler output and returns verdict on the step. The verdict may be correct (the proof compiled and its natural language description is faithful to it), mathematical error (the call names the first failing step and assigns it an error class), or syntax error (the call gets single attempt to patch the corresponding Lean step without changing the mathematics, and the patched proof is kept only if it then compiles). At this stage, the proof may also be discarded due to an ill-posed statement, malformed output, or prose and formal proof that disagree. proof that compiles is labeled correct at every step. Otherwise, the first failing step and every step after it are labeled incorrect, since nothing that builds on an unestablished step is established either. On steps that are true but inadequately justified, this approach can differ from ProcessBench [Zheng et al., 2025], which counts missing justification as an error only when it affects the validity of the solution (Appendix G).

sections.title: 2.1 LeanPRM Corpus
sections.content: Stage 2 produces labeled proof for 13,940 of these statements, and 13,007 remain after the lexical filters and the removal of duplicate and empty proofs. After the quality control described below, LeanPRM contains 10,634 natural-language proofs, 6,370 correct and 4,264 incorrect, with 152,005 labeled steps, obtained with no human annotation. Of these, 98% come from NuminaMath-LEAN and Lean-Workbook. Table 4 in Appendix breaks the corpus down by source and split. Error taxonomy. Stage 2 assigns each reasoning error one of ten classes. Six describe mathematical faults: unjustified assumptions, invalid inequality bounds, wrong witnesses or constructions, missing cases or side conditions, faulty algebraic identities, and errors in modular or divisibility reasoning. The other four describe failures of the formalization rather than of the mathematics. 4 Examples of these errors include lemma applied where its formal hypotheses do not hold, rewrite in the wrong direction, automation asked to close goal it cannot, and residual class for anything else. Appendix gives the definitions the classifier works from. Table 1: Blind audit of flagged steps, 30 per class (all formalization-side classes and the two largest mathematical ones). Judged sound: correct and justified. Share of errors: fraction of incorrect proofs in the unfiltered pool. Formalization-side steps are mostly sound. Mathematical steps are mostly not sound. Quality control. We checked the automatic Stage 2 labels, rather than manual annotations, with two blind audits using Claude Opus 5 as the judge. The judge never saw our labels (prompts in Appendix I). In the first audit, the judge read 100 stratified proofs from the unfiltered pool and named the first incorrect step, if any. It returned usable answer for 99 of them. It disputed 1 of the 52 proofs we label correct. Of the 47 we label incorrect, it found an error in 27 and none in 20. The second audit shows where that disagreement comes from  (Table 1)  . Among 30 flagged steps per class, steps in the formalization-side classes, 35.8% of the incorrect attempts in the pool, were judged sound in 77% to 93% of cases, while steps in the mathematical classes were judged sound less than half the time. We therefore remove every attempt whose first failure is formalization-side, so every negative in LeanPRM carries mathematical error class. We additionally use lexical filters to make sure the natural language proofs do not reference Lean and remove incorrect proofs whose failing step states its own error (Appendix B). sections.title: 2.2 LeanPRM-Bench
sections.content: LeanPRM-Bench is held-out set of 200 theorems, 100 with correct proof and 100 with an incorrect one. No benchmark theorem appears in the training data. proof is labeled correct if its Lean code compiles and reviewing model confirms that the natural-language steps match the formal proof. Every incorrect proof first fails at mathematical error (Appendix B). The benchmark is hard for current models: prompted with the same instructions, four commercial models reach 71.7 to 80.3 mean exact step-label accuracy over three independent runs. In their original reference runs, all four mislabel the same 26 proofs. We report exact step-label accuracy, the fraction of proofs labeled correctly at every step, and verdict accuracy, the fraction with the correct whole-proof verdict. We release LeanPRM-Bench with its step labels, error classes and formal proofs.

sections.title: 3 Experiments
sections.content: Training. The verifier reads theorem and its numbered steps, writes its reasoning, and then gives each step label, correct or incorrect, and the proof an overall verdict (prompt in Appendix I). We train Qwen3 models [Yang et al., 2025] with 0.6B, 4B and 8B parameters, in thinking mode, with group relative policy optimization [GRPO, Shao et al., 2024]. For each proof we sample eight responses at temperature 1, normalize their rewards within the group, and use the normalized reward as the advantage of every token in the response. The importance ratio is clipped to [0.8, 1.26], and KL penalty with coefficient 103 keeps the policy close to the initial model. Each update uses 64 proofs and learning rate of 106. Every trained model in the main comparison gets 500 updates with this configuration. The PRM800K baseline changes the training data. The NuminaMath solver 5 also replaces the verification reward with final-answer reward. Those 500 updates cover 32, 000 proofs: 3.12 passes over the 10,264 LeanPRM training proofs and 0.45 over the 70,502 PRM800K training proofs. Appendix lists every hyperparameter. Reward. Let Rc be the fraction of truly correct steps that the verifier labels correct and Ri the fraction of truly incorrect steps that it labels incorrect, each set to 1 when there are no such steps. With predicted verdict ˆv and true verdict v, the reward is = 0.7 Rstep + 0.3 1[ˆv = v], (cid:40) Rstep = Rc Ri 1[every step labeled correct] otherwise. if the proof contains an error, (1) On proof containing both correct and incorrect steps, the product rules out both constant-label shortcuts. Labeling every step correct gives Ri = 0, and labeling every step incorrect gives Rc = 0. If the first step is incorrect, all steps are incorrect under our labeling convention and the empty-class recall is 1. For the proof in Figure 1, whose steps 5 and 6 are incorrect, verifier that flags only step 6 gets Rc = 1 and Ri = 1/2, so Rstep = 0.5 and, with the verdict necessarily incorrect, = 0.65. The reward is 0 when the output is malformed, has no reasoning section, or gives verdict that contradicts its own step labels. Evaluation. We evaluate on LeanPRM-Bench and on four external benchmarks, each on its full evaluation set, apart from the 13 context-length exclusions on IMO-GradingBench described in Appendix E, and with one metric per benchmark. We use Hard2Verify [Pandit et al., 2025] (responselevel balanced accuracy), ProcessBench [Zheng et al., 2025] (F1, the harmonic mean of accuracy on errors and correct solutions, averaged over its four subsets, 3,400 test cases), PRMBench [Song et al., 2025] (first-error accuracy over 6,216 rows, not its default PRMScore) and IMO-GradingBench [Luong et al., 2025] (balanced accuracy on the grade binarized to fully correct or not, instead of its four-way accuracy, since our verifiers give binary verdict and only about 30% of its proofs are graded correct). We use first-error accuracy on PRMBench because PRMScore scores each step against labels that mark only the erroneous steps as incorrect, so it would penalize every model for following our instruction to label all steps after the first error incorrect. All models get the same prompt layout and label parser, with hosted-response formatting normalization described in Appendix E. response that fails to parse counts as wrong. We report means over three runs, using decoding seeds 42, 43, and 44 at temperature 1 for open-weight models and independent hosted runs for commercial models (Appendix E). Baselines. We compare with the untrained Qwen3-4B and with two models trained by the same recipe on other data: one on PRM800K [Lightman et al., 2023], converted to our step-label format (PRM800K-Verifier-4B), and one with reinforcement learning on solving 19,200 NuminaMath problems with final-answer reward (NuminaMath-Solver-4B), which tests whether verification ability comes from mathematical reinforcement learning alone. For reference we also prompt four commercial models with the same instructions: Claude Sonnet 5, Opus 5 and Fable 5.1 through the Anthropic API with extended thinking, and GPT-5.6 Sol through the Codex command-line interface with every tool disabled (Appendix E). Both trained baselines change little on their own validation data over the second half of their 500 updates (Figure 4, middle), so the 500 step budget is reasonable setting.

sections.title: 4 Related Work
sections.content: LeanPRM draws on two lines of work. Process supervision trains verifiers on step-level labels, which mostly come from human annotators or from the outcomes of sampled continuations. Formal mathematics offers exact checking, which has mainly been used to train and evaluate provers that write Lean. We connect the two by using Lean only to label natural-language proofs, and the verifier we train never sees formal proof. Process supervision. Lightman et al. [2023] scaled up process supervision for mathematical reasoning with human step-level annotations. Subsequent work reduces this annotation cost by deriving process supervision from outcome signals: Math-Shepherd estimates step quality from the correctness of sampled continuations [Wang et al., 2023], OmegaPRM scales such annotation using tree search [Luo et al., 2024], and RL Tango trains generative process verifier directly from outcomelevel rewards [Zha et al., 2025]. Outcome-trained verifiers were introduced for word problems by Cobbe et al. [2021], and Uesato et al. [2022] ran the first comprehensive comparison of processand outcome-based feedback on natural-language task; later work scales automated step labels through rollouts and value estimates [Lu et al., 2024, Setlur et al., 2024], casts verification as generation [Zhang et al., 2024], and distills practical lessons for training process reward models [Zhang et al., 2025a], 9 Table 3: Sources of step-level labels in prior work and in LeanPRM. For each method we give the origin of its step labels and whether they avoid human annotation, cover open-ended naturallanguage proofs, give each failing step mathematical error type, and train verifier that reads the proof text. Only LeanPRM does all four. Method Step labels from PRM800K [Lightman et al., 2023] Human annotators Math-Shepherd [Wang et al., 2023] Rollouts OmegaPRM [Luo et al., 2024] FoVer [Kamoi et al., 2025] Safe [Liu et al., 2025] TP-as-a-Judge [Leang et al., 2025] LeanTutor [Patel et al., 2026] Rollouts (tree search) Z3, Isabelle Lean 4 Lean 4 (per solution) Lean 4 LeanPRM (ours) Lean 4 No human step labels Open-ended proofs Error classes Trained verifier and such verifiers are what makes test-time search effective [Ma et al., 2023, Snell et al., 2024], since models struggle to correct their own reasoning without external feedback [Huang et al., 2023]. These approaches obtain labels from the model-generated solution distribution, either through human judgment or through rollout statistics. We instead obtain them from an external decision procedure, which makes the correctness criterion explicit and independent of the model being supervised. In this direction, FoVer [Kamoi et al., 2025] is closely related. It trains process reward models on formal reasoning traces labeled with Z3 and Isabelle, then evaluates their transfer to natural-language reasoning. LeanPRM instead trains directly on natural-language competition proofs paired with Lean tactics and distinguishes mathematical errors from formalization failures. Safe [Liu et al., 2025] checks each step of natural-language solution in Lean 4 to score solutions at inference, and Theorem Prover as Judge [Leang et al., 2025] uses Lean verdicts on whole solutions to select fine-tuning data. Formal mathematics. Lean 4 [de Moura and Ullrich, 2021] and Mathlib [The mathlib Community, 2020] have been widely used to construct data and train formal theorem provers [Lin et al., 2025a, Yang et al., 2023] and autoformalizers [Gao et al., 2024]. Provers such as DeepSeek-Prover [Ren et al., 2025, Xin et al., 2024], Kimina-Prover [Wang et al., 2025], Goedel-Prover-V2 [Lin et al., 2025b] and Seed-Prover [Chen et al., 2025] learn from proof-assistant feedback, Lean-STaR interleaves informal thoughts with tactics [Lin et al., 2024], and miniF2F and PutnamBench track their progress [Tsoukalas et al., 2024, Zheng et al., 2021]. Autoformalization [Wu et al., 2022] and formalized problem sets such as Lean Workbook [Ying et al., 2024] supply the statements, informal proofs can be mapped to formal proof sketches [Jiang et al., 2022], and Yang et al. [2024] survey the field. Recent work also uses formal verification to evaluate natural-language reasoning [Zhou and Zhang, 2025], to check key steps during inference [Ospanov et al., 2025], or to provide training signals for natural-language reasoning [Cao et al., 2026] and formal proof generation [Kim and Yun, 2026]. DeepTheorem uses automatically verifiable theorem outcomes [Zhang et al., 2025b], while DeepSeekMath-V2 trains natural-language provers with learned proof verifier [Shao et al., 2025]. LeanTutor [Patel et al., 2026] checks student proofs step by step in Lean to give feedback. Our work instead uses such step labels, at scale, as training data for verifier that reads only natural language, providing supervision that is more scalable than expert annotation and more mechanically grounded than model judgments. Our use of the checker differs in that the object being supervised is natural-language reasoning: the formal proof is never the models output and never appears in its input. 10 Verifier training and evaluation. Our verifiers are trained with group-relative policy optimization [Shao et al., 2024], variant of PPO [Schulman et al., 2017] that DeepSeek-R1 scaled to reasoning [DeepSeek-AI et al., 2025], implemented in VERL [Sheng et al., 2024]. The prover-verifier framing follows Anil et al. [2021], as applied to language models by Kirchner et al. [2024], and critic models that surface errors in model outputs [McAleese et al., 2024] are the closest analog outside mathematics. Evaluation of step-level verifiers has been addressed by ProcessBench [Zheng et al., 2025], which measures identification of the first erroneous step in short solutions to grade-school, competition and Olympiad-level problems, including GSM8K and MATH [Cobbe et al., 2021, Hendrycks et al., 2021], PRMBench [Song et al., 2025], which probes specific failure modes of process reward models, and Hard2Verify [Pandit et al., 2025], which targets proofs whose correctness is difficult to establish. Appendix discusses how benchmarks annotation convention can interact with the convention used in training.

sections.title: 5 Conclusion
sections.content: We introduced LeanPRM, framework that uses Lean to label every step of natural-language proofs, trained verifiers on its corpus of 10,634 proofs, and released held-out benchmark, LeanPRM-Bench. With the same recipe and training budget, these verifiers outperform verifiers trained on the human labels of PRM800K on four of five benchmarks, and they pick better proofs at test time. formal tool can therefore be used to train verifiers for informal reasoning, without autoformalization. Lean is needed only once, offline, to build the training data, and the verifier it produces checks natural language directly. Limitations. LeanPRM separates failures of the formal encoding from errors in the mathematics, and the audit in Section 2.1 shows that the classes it removes consist mostly of sound steps. The separation itself relies on models classification, checked with single judge model on sample, so some borderline steps may still carry the wrong label. We compared Lean labels with the human labels of PRM800K but did not train on the same proofs labeled by an LLM judge, so we cannot yet say how much of the gain comes from the labels and how much from training on proof-style data. LeanPRM-Bench comes from the same pipeline and the same Claude generators as the training data, so the four external benchmarks carry most of the evidence that the verifiers generalize. Because negative examples come from Claudes own mistakes, they may cover narrower range of errors than proof verifier should detect. Future work. We believe the same methodology for generating verifier training data could carry over to other open-ended tasks that have no final answer but contain parts an exact checker can verify, such as test suites for code or simulators for science. Within mathematics, generating new theorem statements would let the corpus grow beyond existing formal collections in size and difficulty. Verifiers trained on LeanPRM could also serve as reward models, for training provers and for giving step-level feedback on proofs too hard for people to check, which becomes more important as models approach and exceed human expertise.

sections.title: A Error classes
sections.content: Stage 2 assigns each reasoning error one of ten classes, defined in its instructions as follows. The mathematical classes are: algebraic identity error, false or invalid algebraic manipulation; invalid inequality bound, bound with the wrong direction or without justification; bad witness or construction, wrong witness for an existential claim or an invalid construction; modular or divisibility error, incorrect modular arithmetic or divisibility reasoning; missing case or side condition, required case or side condition that is omitted; and unjustified assumption, claim asserted without support from the preceding steps. The formalization-side classes are: theorem misapplication, lemma applied where its hypotheses do not hold as stated; wrong rewrite direction, an invalid or reversed rewrite or substitution; automation misuse, claim that automation discharges goal it cannot; and other, failure not captured by the classes above. Attempts whose failure was recorded without class are reported as unclassified. 16 Data sources, filtering and splits Theorem statements come from difficulty-filtered subset of NuminaMath-LEAN [Wang et al., 2025], Lean-Workbook [Lin et al., 2025a, Ying et al., 2024], Pythagoras [Leang et al., 2026], Herald [Gao et al., 2024], ProofNet [Azerbayev et al., 2023] and FormalQualBench [Math Inc., 2026]. Table 4 gives the composition of LeanPRM by source and by split. Table 4: Size of LeanPRM by source (top) and by split (bottom); each theorem contributes one proof. NuminaMath supplies most of the incorrect proofs and Lean-Workbook most of the correct ones. Correct Incorrect Total NuminaMath Lean-Workbook Pythagoras Herald ProofNet Training Validation LeanPRM-Bench LeanPRM 1,334 4,787 230 13 6,170 100 100 6,370 3,978 284 1 1 0 4,094 70 100 5,312 5,071 231 14 6 10,264 170 4,264 10,634 Theorem identity is defined modulo the declaration name, and every split is drawn by theorem group so that alpha-renamed restatements cannot cross boundary. The training split holds 10,264 theorems, 6,170 with correct proof and 4,094 with an incorrect one; within each source the smaller verdict cell is oversampled to parity, giving training view of 17,670 rows. The validation split holds 170 theorems (100 correct, 70 incorrect) and LeanPRM-Bench 200, 100 of each verdict. LeanPRMBench was fixed before the class-based filter of Section 2.1, and 30 of its incorrect proofs turned out to have formalization-side first error. We replaced them with 30 incorrect proofs from the validation split whose first error is mathematical, which is why the validation split holds 170 theorems, and re-evaluated every system on the replaced items. The validation curves in Figure 4 were recorded during training on the original 200-theorem validation split, which still contained those 30 proofs. No model was trained on them, and none of the models compared at 500 updates was selected on validation. LeanPRM-Verifier-4B is the exception. Its second stage was stopped at the best checkpoint on an earlier validation split that held 17 of these 30 proofs. Lexical filters. Two lexical checks guard the prose. During generation, an attempt is regenerated if any natural-language step uses one of the following terms as whole word, matched caseinsensitively: lean, tactic, compiler, syntax, solver, automation, automated, verifier, engine, linarith, nlinarith, field_simp, norm_num, aesop, omega. No proof in LeanPRM contains any of them. When the splits are built, an incorrect proof is removed if its first failing step announces its own error with phrases such as unjustified, invalid, false or does not follow, since such text would give the label away. This second check removed 55.2% of the incorrect proofs from the earlier joint procedure and 2.3% of those from the blind procedure. The Lean lines written in Stage 1 are not filtered for sorry, admit or native_decide, which appear in 605 proofs of LeanPRM. Lean accepts sorry/admit as placeholders. native_decide is not one. lexical audit found one positive training proof with explicit sorry, retained in the experiments, and no explicit placeholders in positive validation or 17 benchmark proofs. Transitive dependencies were not checked. Only the repairs made in Stage 2 are barred from using any of the three.

sections.title: C Proofs the frontier models misjudge
sections.content: In the original reference run of each commercial system, 26 of the 200 proofs in LeanPRM-Bench are mislabeled by all four systems. LeanPRM-Verifier-4B labels 8 of them exactly, six incorrect proofs and two correct ones, and over three decoding seeds it labels 29.5% of the 26 exactly, against 7.7% for the untrained model and 11.5% for PRM800K-Verifier-4B. The reverse case, all four commercial systems right and the trained model wrong, covers 12 of the 128 proofs on which all four are right. Figures 6 and 7 show two of the eight and Figure 8 one of the twelve; the remaining cases follow the checkers conventions, such as treating an argument that stops before its conclusion as incorrect at its last step. 18 Figure 6: proof the trained verifier labels exactly and no commercial system does. Step 5 asserts, by an unelaborated strong induction, that any smooth set of numbers yields at least (n 512)/2 disjoint pairs with equal parity vectors; the argument as written does not justify the count, the checker fails at this step, and the class is unjustified assumption. Sonnet 5, Fable 5.1 and PRM800KVerifier-4B accept every step, Opus 5 and GPT-5.6 Sol first object at step 6, and LeanPRM-Verifier-4B flags step 5. 19 Figure 7: An incomplete proof. The argument establishes the summed inequality and defines at step 19, then stops without producing the two distinct zeros. Under the convention of Section 2 the final step of an argument that stops short is incorrect; every other system accepts all nineteen steps, and LeanPRM-Verifier-4B flags the last. Figure 8: The reverse case. Step 8 claims Lagrange-type identity with the wrong coefficient on the first square, so the checkers ring normalization fails and the class is algebraic identity error. All four commercial systems and PRM800K-Verifier-4B flag step 8; LeanPRM-Verifier-4B accepts the proof.

sections.title: D Training details
sections.content: Given the theorem and its numbered natural-language steps, the verifier writes reasoning section, one label per step, and verdict, and the verdict must be incorrect whenever any step is labeled incorrect. Let RecC and RecI denote label recall on the steps that are truly correct and truly incorrect. The step reward is RecC RecI when the proof contains an error and otherwise the indicator that every step is predicted correct; the task reward is 0.7 Rstep + 0.3 Rverdict with Rverdict the verdict accuracy, and malformed output, missing reasoning section, or an inconsistent verdict scores zero. On an incorrect proof with both label classes, the product penalizes both the all-correct and the all-incorrect prediction. All models are optimized with group-relative policy optimization, eight responses per prompt sampled at temperature 1, batch size 64, learning rate 106, KL coefficient 103, and 6,656-token response limit, on four H100 80GB GPUs, with validation and checkpoints every 50 updates. LeanPRM-Verifier-4B is single run continued across three stages of data: 532 updates on an earlier pool of 3,449 training proofs produced by joint generation procedure, 750 updates on the unfiltered pool of Section 2.1 (its best validation checkpoint of 808), and 300 updates on LeanPRM, 1,582 updates in total. Every LeanPRM verifier in Table 5, and PRM800K-Verifier-4B and NuminaMathSolver-4B, trains from its base checkpoint for 500 updates. The 8B model uses the same configuration with parameter and optimizer offloading and rollouts tensor-parallel across two GPUs.

sections.title: E Evaluation details
sections.content: The held-out split is scored by exact step-label accuracy, the fraction of proofs whose every label is predicted correctly, and by verdict accuracy. Hard2Verify is scored by response-level balanced accuracy over its 200 problems, ProcessBench by the mean F1 over its four subsets on all 3,400 test cases, and PRMBench by first-error accuracy on all 6,216 rows. On IMO-GradingBench the four-way human grade is binarized as fully correct against everything else, candidates are split into steps at paragraph boundaries with an even merge above thirty steps, and 13 of the 1,000 candidates exceed the context budget and are dropped, leaving 987. Every model receives the same prompt layout and label parser. Hosted responses are normalized for Markdown formatting before failed parses count as incorrect. We report mean and population standard deviation over three runs, using seeds 42, 43, and 44 at temperature 1 and fixed checkpoints for open-weight models and independent hosted runs without controlled seeds for commercial models. The Claude models are run through the Anthropic API with extended thinking at high effort and 16,000-token budget, retrying truncations or refusals once at 32,000 tokens. Fables system prompt omits the thinking-end tag. GPT-5.6 Sol is run through the Codex command-line interface on ChatGPT subscription, one non-interactive call per item at high reasoning effort with the shell, web search and every other tool disabled. Codex prepends its own agent instructions to the papers prompt and does not return the reasoning, so this row is prompted through Codex rather than through the bare API; all 33,009 evaluations across its three runs completed without tool use.

sections.title: G Labeling conventions and ProcessBench
sections.content: We think most of the ProcessBench gap comes from labeling convention, but we have not tested this directly. Our labels mark the first step that is not justified, while ProcessBench counts missing justification as an error only when it affects the validity of the solution, so on true but unjustified step our verifier should flag earlier than the reference. Across three checkpoints of the run behind LeanPRM-Verifier-4B, after 532, 1,282 and 1,332 updates, flags placed strictly before the reference step rise from 158 to 236 to 379. Only the last two checkpoints share training data, so the trend fits the explanation without isolating it; an audit of the early flags would settle it.

sections.content: Three further training examples in the format of Figure 1, chosen to show the three kinds of attempt the pipeline produces. Figure 9: correct attempt: for real t, 2t 1 + t2. Every step elaborates, so every step is labeled correct. The argument is the standard completion of the square, written as four claims each realized by one tactic. Attempts of this kind account for 6,370 of the 10,634 theorems in LeanPRM. 23 Figure 10: reasoning error whose text shows the slip. The statement asks, for 2 and every bound , for some > dividing the sum of the k-th powers of its divisors. The attempt proposes = 1, which cannot exceed an arbitrary , and step 4 concedes as much while trying to discharge the bound anyway. Elaboration fails at that step; Stage 2 assigns the class invalid inequality bound, and steps 4 and 5 are labeled incorrect. 24 Figure 11: An attempt from the labeled pool that is not part of LeanPRM. The statement is that implies 2d 1 2n 1. Step 3 invokes the true fact that divides xm ym; the mathematics is sound, but the Lean line names the library lemma in form the pinned Mathlib does not accept, so elaboration fails there and Stage 2 assigns theorem misapplication. The audit judged steps of this class sound in 26 of 30 cases, which is why the formalization-side classes are excluded from the corpus.

They are allowed only as final arithmetic discharge after the preceding steps have made the algebraic situation, case split, divisibility fact, modular computation, or inequality combination explicit enough that the NL remains 1:1 and mathematically informative. - Do not use `sorry`, `admit`, `by_contra!` as placeholder, or any unfinished proof placeholder. - Do not use one opaque tactic to hide the main argument. If proof needs algebra, inequalities, case splits, contradiction, divisibility facts, or modular arithmetic, introduce those facts as explicit intermediate `have`, `calc`, `rw`, or case-analysis steps before any final arithmetic discharge. - The proof must be step-by-step: step 0 is the theorem line ending in `:= by`, and each later step is one Lean tactic or one tightly scoped Lean proof line. - Keep the proof concise. Aim for at most 40 steps and do not split routine 26 rewriting or arithmetic into dozens of tiny steps. - Each step must include natural-language mathematical explanation matching that exact Lean step 1:1 (see rules and example below). - Natural language must explain the mathematics only. Do not mention Lean, tactics, automation, syntax, or the compiler. - The natural language must not describe stronger or more detailed argument than the Lean line actually proves. If the NL says "we write = 4q + 1", the Lean line must actually establish that statement in the corresponding case; if the NL cites an algebraic identity, the Lean line must establish that identity or use it directly. - It is acceptable if the proof attempt is mathematically wrong, but avoid syntax errors and malformed Lean where possible. - Return only JSON. No Markdown fences. [the natural-language rules, worked example, and the JSON schema follow] Stage 2 receives the following instructions together with the ten error classes of Appendix A, the Lean statement, the compiler output, the frozen steps, and JSON schema for its verdict. Classify this immutable Stage-1 Lean/NL proof attempt after Lean verification and, only when appropriate, return minimal surface-form Lean syntax patches. Stage 1 is the true blind attempt. Its natural-language descriptions and mathematical plan are frozen. You MUST NOT rewrite, improve, complete, or correct them. Compiler feedback is available only for classification and private syntax repair; it must never leak into the natural-language trajectory. This is the second and final LLM call for this datapoint. Decide one verdict: - "correct": Lean verification already SUCCEEDED and the natural-language proof is faithful to the Lean proof. - "reasoning_error": Lean verification FAILED because the mathematical proof attempt is false, unjustified, or incomplete at the first failing step. This includes missing branch, missing direction, unclosed goal, or an argument that stops before proving the theorem. These are valuable natural solver failures and MUST be retained as reasoning errors, not discarded. If the attempt simply stops with an unclosed goal, use its final provided step as `first_error_step`, not step 0. - "repair": Lean verification FAILED for purely MECHANICAL/code reason while the underlying mathematics is VALID, such as punctuation, parentheses, namespace, renamed identifier with exactly the same proposition, or an explicit type or coercion annotation expressing the same term. Return only the changed Lean lines. - "discard": the statement is ill-posed, the output is malformed, or the NL and Lean silently describe different mathematics. Do NOT discard merely because the proof is incomplete or would need substantial new mathematics to finish. REPAIR RULES (only when verdict is "repair"): - Fix ONLY surface-form Lean syntax or elaboration. Do NOT change the mathematics. - Do NOT alter step 0 in any way. - Do NOT weaken the theorem, and do NOT use `sorry`, `admit`, `native_decide`, or any placeholder/cheat tactic. - Do NOT add, remove, merge, split, or reorder steps. - Do NOT change proposition, expression, witness, assumption, case split, intermediate claim, tactic kind, tactic strategy, or tactic arguments that carry mathematical content. - Do NOT swap tactics or add hints, facts, automation, or "small nudges." - If it cannot compile without adding or changing substantive mathematics, use "reasoning_error" when the attempt is incomplete or mathematically invalid. 27 For any verdict other than "repair", return no syntax patches.
